paragraphs.heading: What counts as one
paragraphs.text: An optical instrument is a device that works on light, whether you think of that light as waves or as photons. It does one of two jobs. Either it improves an image so that a person can see it better, or it examines the light itself to work out its properties. Familiar instruments of this kind include periscopes, microscopes, telescopes and cameras.

paragraphs.heading: The first instruments
paragraphs.text: The earliest optical instruments did the first job, making things look bigger. Telescopes magnified scenes that were far away, and microscopes magnified things that were very tiny. Since the time of Galileo and Van Leeuwenhoek, both kinds have been improved a great deal. They have also been pushed beyond their original range into other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: Instruments for seeing
paragraphs.text: Some optical instruments are built to be carried. Binoculars are a generally compact instrument made for both eyes and designed for use on the move. A camera can also be counted as an optical instrument. The pinhole camera and the camera obscura are very simple examples of the type.

paragraphs.heading: Instruments that measure light
paragraphs.text: The second job, analysing light, turns up in places you might not expect. A DNA sequencer can be thought of as an optical instrument. A light-emitting tag called a fluorochrome is attached to a specific nucleotide of a DNA strand, and the machine analyses the colour and intensity of the light that tag gives off. Instruments based on surface plasmon resonance are another example: they use refractometry to measure and study how biological molecules interact with each other.

paragraphs.heading: A broad family
paragraphs.text: Set side by side, these examples show how wide the family is. At one end sits the camera obscura, one of the very simplest kinds of camera. At the other sits the DNA sequencer, which studies the colour and brightness of light from tags attached to a DNA strand. Telescopes and microscopes, the first members, belong on the side that improves images, while sequencers and instruments built on refractometry belong on the side that analyses light.
